By one week, the interval expands to 65 points (about 16% total width), incorporating the possibility of scheduled data releases, earnings, or macro events within the week. On the downside, a liquidity event, a credit scare, or a sharp deterioration in sentiment could break below 330. These tail risks are real but were judged low-probability at the time of the forecast, hence why they sit outside the 90% confidence interval rather than inside it.

It's worth noting that these intervals represent my stated 90% confidence, meaning I explicitly acknowledged a 10% probability of outcomes falling outside the range. Given typical fat tails in financial markets — where extreme moves occur more frequently than normal distributions would predict — the true probability of an outside outcome may be somewhat higher than 10% in practice. Anyone using these forecasts should treat the confidence intervals as reasonable planning ranges rather than hard boundaries, and remain alert to the possibility that the realized outcome surprises even a well-calibrated forecast.
